title: Apple Faces Fraud Lawsuit Over iCloud Private Relay IP Address Leaks
excerpt: A proposed class action accuses Apple of deceiving iCloud+ subscribers after WebKit flaws exposed real IP addresses despite privacy promises.
body:
• The Clarkson Law Firm has filed a proposed class action accusing Apple of fraud and false advertising over security flaws in iCloud Private Relay.
  • Three WebKit vulnerabilities—involving passkey sign-ins, DNS prefetching, and WebTransport—can expose users' real IP addresses even with Private Relay enabled.
  • The same firm previously secured a $250 million settlement from Apple over misleading Siri AI features.
  • The lawsuit seeks at least $5 million in relief and an injunction against Apple's alleged false marketing of the privacy feature.

Apple is facing a proposed class action lawsuit accusing it of fraud and false advertising over security flaws in iCloud Private Relay, the premium privacy feature marketed as a shield for users' IP addresses and browsing activity.

The suit, filed by California resident Edward Rickman in federal court, alleges Apple knowingly sold iCloud+ subscriptions with privacy promises that did not hold up. Rickman purchased the service specifically for access to Private Relay, which Apple advertises as a tool to "Hide your IP address and browsing activity in Safari and protect your unencrypted internet traffic."

Three WebKit Flaws at the Center

The lawsuit points to three distinct WebKit vulnerabilities that security researchers detailed in early August 2026. The most critical involves passkey sign-ins: a website can trigger a passkey validation check that gets handled by the device's operating system rather than Safari, completely bypassing Private Relay's proxy servers. In some cases, this occurs without even displaying a passkey prompt, meaning users have no indication their IP address has been exposed.

https://x.com/PKNewsland/status/2088479125824835909

Two additional flaws compound the problem. DNS prefetching in iOS 26 can resolve hostnames through the normal DNS path rather than through a proxy, exposing DNS server information. The WebTransport protocol, also introduced in iOS 26, can open direct HTTP/3 connections that reveal a user's real IP address.

Because WebKit powers every browser on iOS—not just Safari—the exposure extends to all mobile browsers on iPhones and iPads.

"For Apple's iCloud users to now learn that for years they were paying Apple a premium for a protection that simply didn't work, exposing them to the very tracking, profiling, and targeting Apple warned them about, is an outrageous violation and betrayal of consumer trust and law."

— Tim Giordano, Partner, Clarkson Law Firm

The Clarkson Law Firm's Track Record

The lawsuit is being led by the Clarkson Law Firm, which has recent history taking on Apple over consumer protection issues. The firm previously secured a $250 million settlement from Apple over claims it misled consumers about Siri's AI capabilities. That case was resolved in December 2025, though payout details were not disclosed until May 2026.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=IIGYykbb6VI

Apple charges between $0.99 and $59.99 per month for iCloud+ subscriptions, depending on storage tier. The class would include all US citizens who paid for iCloud+ and enabled Private Relay within a specified timeframe. The lawsuit seeks an injunction on Apple's marketing of the feature, attorneys' fees, and at least $5 million in relief for class members.

Apple's Privacy Brand Under Pressure

Apple first unveiled iCloud Private Relay at its Worldwide Developers Conference in June 2021, releasing it later that year with an iOS update. The company has built its brand heavily around privacy, making this lawsuit particularly pointed. Apple has told media outlets it is investigating the security researchers' findings, but has not commented publicly on the lawsuit itself.

Security experts note that while Private Relay was never intended as a full VPN replacement, the marketing language Apple used implied comprehensive IP address protection that the WebKit flaws clearly undermined. Users concerned about IP exposure are being advised to use dedicated VPN services until Apple patches the vulnerabilities.

What's Next

The case will proceed through the Northern District of California, where Apple faces multiple ongoing legal battles including its App Store dispute with Epic Games. For the millions of iCloud+ subscribers who enabled Private Relay, the outcome could set a precedent for how tech companies are held accountable for privacy feature marketing.
